title: 6. Merging & Joining Data
text: In SAS, merging requires you to PROC SORT both datasets first. If you forget, things break. In R, dplyr joins do not require sorting. They use a hash join algorithm, which is generally faster and safer.

title: 6. Merging & Joining Data
text:
Left Join
Keep all rows from the Left table, match rows from the Right. Unmatched become NA. Equivalent to SAS Merge (A, B) with if a.
library(dplyr)

# Join DM and AE by Subject ID
dm_ae <- left_join(dm, ae, by = "USUBJID")

title: 6. Merging & Joining Data
text:
Inner Join
Keep only rows present in both tables. Equivalent to SAS Merge (A, B) with if a and b.
patients_with_events <- inner_join(dm, ae, by = "USUBJID")

title: 6. Merging & Joining Data
text:
Full Join
Keep rows from either table. Equivalent to SAS Merge (A, B).
all_data <- full_join(dm, ae, by = "USUBJID")

title: 6. Merging & Joining Data
text:
Semi Join
Keep rows in A that have a match in B. (Like a WHERE EXISTS SQL subquery).
# Keep patients in DM who have at least one AE
patients_with_ae <- semi_join(dm, ae, by = "USUBJID")

title: 6. Merging & Joining Data
text:
Anti Join
Keep rows in A that do not have a match in B. (Great for finding “orphan” records).
# Keep patients in DM who have ZERO AEs
healthy_patients <- anti_join(dm, ae, by = "USUBJID")

title: 3. Data Structures: Vectors & Frames
text:
In SAS, almost everything is a dataset. In R, you have lower-level building blocks.


The fundamental unit in R. Even a single number is a vector of length 1. Vectors must be of the same type (numeric, character, logical).
# Numeric vector
ages <- c(25, 30, 45, 22)

# Character vector
names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
Note: R is 1-indexed, just like SAS. ages[1] is 25.



Lists can contain anything: vectors, datasets, other lists, models. They are flexible containers.
my_patient <- list(
  id = "1001",
  visits = c("Screening", "Baseline", "Week 4"),
  demographics = data.frame(age = 45, sex = "M")
)



This is your SAS Dataset. It is technically a list of vectors of equal length.

data.frame: The base R version.
tibble: The modern (“tidyverse”) version. It prints nicer and is stricter (doesn’t change variable names or types unexpectedly).

library(tibble)

dm <- tibble(
  USUBJID = c("001", "002", "003"),
  ARM = c("Placebo", "Active", "Placebo"),
  AGE = c(45, 52, 38)
)



Factors are used for categorical data. They look like strings but are stored as integers with labels. This is similar to SAS Formats.
sex <- factor(c("M", "F", "F", "M"), levels = c("F", "M"))



In SAS, numeric missing is .. In R, it is NA. Important: NA propagates. 5 + NA equals NA. You often need na.rm = TRUE in functions.
mean(c(1, 2, NA)) # Returns NA
mean(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE) # Returns 1.5




If you try to put a character string into a numeric vector, what happens?
What is the R equivalent of a SAS format?

title: 4. Data Import & Export
text:
The haven package is the gold standard for reading .sas7bdat and .xpt files.
library(haven)
library(here)

# Reading a SAS dataset
# equivalent to: set mylib.adae;
adae <- read_sas(here("data", "adae.sas7bdat"))

# Reading an XPT file (common for FDA submissions)
dm_xpt <- read_xpt(here("data", "dm.xpt"))


haven imports SAS labels as an attribute called label. It imports SAS formats as format.
You can view these with:
# View variable label
attr(adae$AESEV, "label")

title: 8. Tables & Reporting
text:
The gt package allows you to construct tables by adding layers, similar to how ggplot2 builds plots.
library(gt)
library(dplyr)

# Prepare data
summary_table <- adae %>%
  group_by(AESOC) %>%
  summarise(
    n_events = n(),
    n_subjects = n_distinct(USUBJID)
  )

# Create Table
summary_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Adverse Events by SOC"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    AESOC = "System Organ Class",
    n_events = "Total Events",
    n_subjects = "Total Subjects"
  )

title: 10. Package Development
text:
In SAS, you might rely on server configuration. In R, packages change versions. renv (R Environment) creates a lockfile (renv.lock) that records exactly which version of every package you used.

renv::init(): Initialize a project.
renv::snapshot(): Save the current state of packages to the lockfile.
renv::restore(): Reinstall packages exactly as recorded in the lockfile.

This ensures that your code runs 5 years from now.

title: 5. Data Manipulation (dplyr)
text:
SAS Operation
R (dplyr)




KEEP/DROP
select()


WHERE
filter()


IF ... THEN ...
mutate() + if_else()/case_when()


BY
group_by()


PROC SORT
arrange()


RENAME
rename()


PROC MEANS/FREQ
summarise()

title: 5. Data Manipulation (dplyr)
text:
Filter (WHERE)
# numeric condition
filter(dm, AGE >= 18)

# string condition
filter(dm, ARM == "Placebo")

# multiple conditions (AND)
filter(dm, AGE >= 18, SEX == "F")

# OR condition
filter(dm, ARM == "Placebo" | ARM == "Active")

title: 5. Data Manipulation (dplyr)
text:
Arrange (PROC SORT)
# Ascending
arrange(dm, USUBJID)

# Descending
arrange(dm, desc(AGE))

title: 5. Data Manipulation (dplyr)
text:
Select (KEEP/DROP)
# Keep specific columns
select(dm, USUBJID, AGE)

# Drop columns
select(dm, -RFSTDTC)

# Select helper functions
select(dm, starts_with("AE"))

title: 5. Data Manipulation (dplyr)
text:
Mutate (Variable Creation)
dm_new <- dm %>%
  mutate(
    # Simple arithmetic
    AGE_MONTHS = AGE * 12,
    
    # Conditional logic (if/else)
    AGE_GROUP = if_else(AGE >= 65, "Elderly", "Adult"),
    
    # Complex logic (CASE statement)
    BMI_CAT = case_when(
      BMI < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
      BMI < 25 ~ "Normal",
      BMI < 30 ~ "Overweight",
      TRUE ~ "Obese" # The "Else" clause
    )
  )

title: 1. Introduction: SAS vs R
text:
You are likely an expert in SAS. You know how to manipulate data, generate reports, and debug macros. So why learn R?

Open Source: R is free and has a massive community contributing packages.
Vectorization: R operations often apply to entire columns at once, reducing the need for explicit loops.
Graphics: ggplot2 offers unparalleled flexibility for data visualization.
Modern Workflows: R integrates seamlessly with Git, extensive testing frameworks, and reproducible reporting tools like Quarto.

title: 1. Introduction: SAS vs R
1. Introduction: SAS vs R
1. Introduction: SAS vs R
text:
3. Disk vs. RAM

SAS: Libraries (LIBNAME) often point to physical files on the hard drive. SAS handles large data by processing it chunk-by-chunk from the disk.
R: Objects live in RAM (Memory). This makes R extremely fast for most datasets but requires different strategies for “Big Data” (e.g., arrow, sparklyr, or databases).

title: 2. The R Ecosystem & Tools
text:
R is the language and the engine.
RStudio is the Integrated Development Environment (IDE). It’s like the “SAS Enterprise Guide” for R, but much more developer-focused.





Source (Top Left): Your “Program Editor”. This is where you write scripts (.R) or Quarto documents (.qmd).
Console (Bottom Left): The “Log” and immediate execution area. You can type commands here to test them, but they aren’t saved.
Environment (Top Right): Shows your “Work Library”. All active dataframes, variables, and functions live here.
Files/Plots/Packages (Bottom Right): File browser, plot viewer, and package manager.

section: Map: Apply function to each element
text:
Map: Apply function to each element
Suppose you have a list of files to read.
library(purrr)
library(readr)

files <- c("data/cohort1.csv", "data/cohort2.csv", "data/cohort3.csv")

# Read all files into a list of dataframes
data_list <- map(files, read_csv)

# Read all files and stack them immediately into one dataframe
all_data <- map_dfr(files, read_csv)
